When she came to the office, she was 5 feet 6 inches tall, weighed 285.4 pounds, and had a body mass index (BMI) of 46. She has health problems related to obesity, which include high blood pressure and high cholesterol.

**PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:** 
Significant for high blood pressure, for which she takes Norvasc and Lopressor. She also has high cholesterol and takes lovastatin for it. She has depression, for which she takes citalopram. She stated she had a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the past before her hysterectomy. She also had past thyroid disease, though the exact details of this are unclear.

**PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:** 
She had her gallbladder removed (cholecystectomy) in 2008 due to gallstones. She also had a hysterectomy in 1994 due to severe bleeding. The patient states she has had no other surgeries on her belly.

**MEDICATIONS:** 
* Norvasc 10 mg by mouth daily
* Lopressor tartrate 50 mg by mouth twice a day
* Lovastatin 10 mg by mouth at bedtime
* Citalopram 10 mg by mouth daily
* Aspirin 500 mg three times a day (currently stopped)
* Vitamin D
* Premarin 0.3 mg one tablet by mouth daily (currently stopped)
* Omega-3 fatty acids
* Vitamin D 50,000 units once a week

**ALLERGIES:** 
The patient states she is not allergic to any medications or latex.

**SOCIAL HISTORY:** 
The patient is a homemaker. She is married and has two children, aged 22 and 28. She has never smoked and never drinks alcohol.

**FAMILY HISTORY:** 
Her father had high blood pressure, diabetes, and cancer, and he passed away from congestive heart failure. Her mother had high blood pressure, cancer, and diabetes, and passed away from cancer. She has two brothers, and one passed away from brain cancer.

**REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:** 
She has swelling in her ankles. She wears glasses and has dentures. She complains of feeling short of breath when she is active. She also has hemorrhoids, has to urinate often at night, and has joint pain when bearing weight. She does not have ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease, bleeding disorders, liver disease, or kidney disease. She does not have chest pain, heart disease, cancer, or a history of stroke.

* **Nervous System:** Muscle strength in her arms and legs is equal on both sides with no focused nerve problems.
* **Lungs:** Breath sounds are clear with no wheezing.
* **Heart:** Regular rate and rhythm with no murmurs or abnormal sounds.
* **Abdomen:** Bowel sounds are present. Her belly is soft, not tender, obese, and not swollen. Scars from her gallbladder surgery are visible. No obvious hernias or enlarged organs.
* **Lower extremities:** Mild swelling (1+ edema). Pulses in the feet (dorsalis pedis) are normal (2+).

**ASSESSMENT:** 
The patient is a 55-year-old woman with a BMI of 46. She has health issues related to obesity, including high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and is being evaluated for gastric bypass surgery. She appears to be an excellent candidate for the surgery and would benefit greatly from surgical weight loss to help manage her weight-related health conditions.

**PLAN:** 
To prepare for surgery, we will run standard baseline lab tests, including baseline vitamin levels. I recommended that the patient get an upper GI series before surgery to check her upper digestive tract anatomy. She will also meet with a dietitian and a psychologist, as is standard for this process. I recommended that she use the Medifast diet for about six to eight weeks to lose 10% of her weight before surgery.

**Patient:** ABC  
**Medical Record #:** 123  
**RE:** Consult letter to Dr. XYZ  

Dear Dr. XYZ,

I saw ABC in the Neuro-Oncology Clinic today for an urgent visit. He has growing concerns about what to do next to treat his brain tumor, anaplastic astrocytoma. 

Over the last few days, he met with you to discuss whether to have radiation therapy for the tumor in the left temporal lobe of his brain. He remains very unsure about doing radiation, for reasons that are not entirely clear. His recent MRI scan shows the tumor is growing. At this point, it is unlikely that any treatment other than radiation will work well. Even though I repeated this to him, he is still worried about possible long-term side effects that do not seem likely right now.

After seeing you, he and his friend wanted to talk about changing his chemotherapy. They brought a list of eight different chemotherapy drugs they want to use within the next two weeks. They also wanted another MRI scan. They hope this plan will cause the tumor to go into remission so he can avoid radiation.

During the visit, I noticed that his speech has gotten worse just in the last week since I last saw him. This is very concerning. Today, for the first time, I also noticed a clear drooping on the right side of his face. There is no doubt that his growing tumor is now causing physical symptoms. This means his body is reaching its limit, and his condition could get much worse very quickly.

I strongly recommended that he start steroid medication and again tried to convince him to get radiation therapy. After talking for an hour, he still refused radiation. However, it is not because he refuses all treatment. Because I told him it would be unethical to use the risky drug plan that he and his friend made up, we agreed on a compromise. 

We decided to restart the chemotherapy drug Temodar at a low, daily dose. The plan is for him to take 75 mg per square meter every day for 21 days out of a 28-day cycle. At the same time, we will stop his current thalidomide medication (100 mg per day). If he can handle the Temodar for one week, we agreed to add another medicine from his list—specifically, Accutane.

While I am very uncomfortable with this treatment plan, as long as we watch him closely, we may be able to do this for a short time. As part of our compromise, he agreed to be evaluated by the radiation team again. This time, he seemed more accepting that radiation will need to happen sooner rather than later. I see this as a positive sign because radiation is the one treatment that can give him a good long-term response.

I will keep you updated on his follow-up care. Please contact me if you have any questions or need more help.

Sincerely,

**REASON FOR NEUROLOGY CONSULTATION:** 
Neck arthritis (cervical spondylosis) and a forward-curving neck deformity (kyphotic deformity). 

**HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:** 
The patient is a 45-year-old African-American woman. Her symptoms started about a year and a half ago with pain in her left shoulder and neck, which has since gone away. She started heavy workouts in November 2005. In March, she suddenly could not feel her right foot on the bathroom floor and saw her primary care doctor. She had a nerve test that showed a pinched nerve (radiculopathy). A lower back MRI was normal. 

She then got a tingling feeling in her right middle toe. The symptoms spread to her knees, elbows, and left middle toe. Next, she felt tingling in her left hand and arm. She feels a little wobbly at the knees and drags her left leg slightly. Her symptoms have been slowly getting worse. She does not know of any cause other than her heavy workouts. She has no bowel or bladder problems. No specific position makes her symptoms better.

She has had two neck MRIs. Surgery to relieve pressure on the spine was discussed with her previously, but she is currently hesitant to have surgery.

**PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:**
1. Migraines with vision changes (ocular migraines).
2. Uterine fibroid removal surgery (myomectomy).
3. Infertility.
4. High blood sugar (hyperglycemia).
5. Asthma.
6. High cholesterol (hypercholesterolemia).

**MEDICATIONS:** 
Lipitor, Pulmicort, Allegra, Xopenex, Patanol, Duac topical gel, Loprox cream, and Rhinocort.

**ALLERGIES:** 
Penicillin and aspirin.

**SOCIAL HISTORY:**
She does not drink or smoke. She is married with two adopted children and works as a paralegal specialist. She used to exercise heavily, but was recently told to stop and now only walks.

**REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:** 
She reports mild blurred vision, but this has happened before and seems linked to her headaches.

**PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:** 
Blood pressure is 138/82, pulse is 90, breathing rate is 14, and weight is 176.5 pounds. Pain score is 0. Her general exam is normal. 

Her neurological exam shows normal thinking and normal cranial nerves (including a normal jaw reflex). She has a mild trembling (postural tremor) in both arms. She has mild decreased feeling and light touch in her right palm, and decreased vibration feeling in both lower legs. Muscle strength tests are normal, but when walking (gait), she shows very subtle weakness on the left side of her body (hemiparesis). Her lower leg reflexes are overly active (hyperreflexia), especially on the left. Babinski reflexes are normal (downgoing).

simplified_output:
**Reason for Visit:** 
A 3-year-old girl is here to be checked for ongoing ear infections in both ears. 

**Symptoms and History:**
* **Signs of ear infections:** Cough, fever, fussiness, and delays in speech and language.
* **How long it has gone on:** She has taken 12 rounds of antibiotics for ear infections.
* **Pain:** Throbbing ear pain.
* **Allergies:** No known drug allergies.
* **Current Medicines:** None.
* **Past Medical History:** Normal.
* **Past Surgeries:** None.
* **Social History:** Goes to a large daycare.
* **Family History:** Her father’s mother had Alzheimer’s disease.
* **Other Systems:** Normal, except for her ears.

**Physical Exam:**
* **Temperature:** 99.6°F 
* **Weight:** 38 pounds
* **General:** A pleasant 3-year-old who looks well-nourished, well-developed, and clean, and is not in distress. Her mother is with her and speaks English well.
* **Head and Face:** Normal head, face, salivary glands, and facial strength.
* **Eyes:** Pupils are normal.
* **Ears, Nose, and Throat (ENT):** 
  * Both eardrums show middle ear infections (otitis media).
  * A tuning fork test shows decreased hearing in both ears.
  * A small amount of fluid is draining from the left ear.
  * Nose, sinuses, lips, teeth, gums, tongue, and throat look normal.
  * The adenoids (glands in the back of the nose) are enlarged.
* **Neck and Lymph Nodes:** Normal. No swollen lymph nodes in the neck or collarbone area.
* **Lungs:** Normal chest shape and breathing. Lungs sound clear.
* **Heart:** Normal heart sounds with no murmurs or abnormal clicks.
* **Nervous System / Mental State:** Cranial nerves and mood are normal.

**Test Results:**
* A hearing test (audiometry) shows a mild hearing loss (30 decibels) caused by problems moving sound through the ear, and a flat tympanogram (a test of ear drum movement).

**Diagnosis:**
* Pus-filled middle ear infections in both ears that have not broken open on their own.
* Enlarged adenoids in both sides.

**Plan:**
* **Surgery:** Scheduled for August 7, 2003, at Children's Hospital as an outpatient (meaning she goes home the same day). She will be put to sleep using general anesthesia. 
* **Procedures:** 
  1. **Myringotomy and tubes:** Small cuts made in the eardrums to place tiny tubes (to drain fluid).
  2. **Adenoidectomy:** Removal of the enlarged adenoids.
* **Consent:** The parent read and signed the surgery consent form. Risks of the surgery and anesthesia were discussed, and the parent's questions were answered.
* **Information Given:** Educational materials about hospital preregistration, middle ear infections, and ear tube surgery were provided.
* **New Prescription:** Augmentin (400 mg-57 mg/5 ml powder). Directions: Take one dose by mouth every 8 hours. Amount: 1 bottle. Refills: 0. Generic substitution: Not allowed.

**Chief Complaint:** Weakness on the left side of the body.

**History:** A 74-year-old right-handed female woke up from a nap at 11:00 AM on November 22, 1992, feeling weak on her left side. She needed support on her left side to walk. She also felt like she was speaking as though she "was drunk." However, she was able to understand what people were saying to her. Her speech problems completely went away by 12:00 noon. She was brought to the UIHC Emergency Treatment Center (ETC) at 8:30 AM on November 23, 1992, for an evaluation.

**Medications:** None.

**Allergies:** Aspirin (ASA) and Penicillin (PCN) both cause a rash.

**Past Medical History:** 
1) High blood pressure (HTN). 
2) Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). 
3) History of hepatitis (unknown type). 
4) Macular degeneration.

**Social History:** Widowed and lives alone. Does not use alcohol, tobacco, or illegal drugs.

**Family History:** Normal.

**Exam:** 
* Blood pressure: 191/89
* Heart rate: 68
* Breathing rate: 16
* Temperature: 37.2°C

**Mental Status:** Awake and alert to person, place, and time. Speech is fluent and clear, without slurred speech. Naming, understanding, and repeating are all normal.

**Cranial Nerves:** Central blind spot in the left eye (old). Mild drooping of the upper left eyelid (old, confirmed by a picture). Weakness in the lower left side of the face.

**Motor:** Mild weakness on the left side of the body (strength is 4+ to 5- on the affected side). Muscle tone was not mentioned in the chart.

**Sensory:** Normal.

**Coordination:** Finger-to-nose and heel-to-knee movements are impaired due to weakness.

**Station:** Left arm drifts downward when held out (pronator drift). No Romberg sign seen.

**Gait:** Walking with a left-sided weakness (hemiparetic gait) and reduced arm swing on the left upper extremity.

**Reflexes:** 3/3+ in the biceps, triceps, and kneecaps. 2/3+ in the ankles, with 3 to 4 beats of brief, non-sustained ankle twitching (clonus) on the left. Plantar reflexes: Left Babinski sign present; right reflex is downward (flexor).

**General Exam:** Grade 2 out of 6 systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border.

**Hospital Course:** Blood sugar (GS), complete blood count (CBC), prothrombin time (PT), partial thromboplastin time (PTT), creatine kinase (CK), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) were all normal. Arterial blood gas (ABG) was 7.4/46/63 on room air. An EKG showed a normal heart rhythm with a right bundle branch block. An MRI of the brain on November 23, 1995 (noted as 11/23/92 elsewhere), showed a stroke (infarction) in the right side of the pons (a part of the brainstem) involving the pyramidal tract. 

She was treated with Ticlopidine 250 mg twice a day. On November 26, 1992, her left-sided weakness got worse. A head CT on November 27, 1992, was normal. She was treated with intravenous (IV) Heparin. This was stopped the next day when her strength returned to the level it was on November 23. 

On November 27, 1992, she developed chest pain (angina). Serial EKGs and heart enzyme blood tests showed she did not have a heart attack (ruled out for MI). A carotid ultrasound (duplex) showed 0-15% narrowing in both internal carotid arteries and normal forward blood flow in both vertebral arteries. An echocardiogram through the chest showed only aortic valve leakage (aortic insufficiency). An echocardiogram through the esophagus showed minor leakage in the mitral and tricuspid valves, and stiffness (fibrosis) of the aortic valve. Calcium deposits (calcification) and a possible blood clot (thrombus) were seen in the descending aorta. Cardiology decided the clot was not a reason to use blood thinners (anticoagulation). 

She was discharged home taking Isordil 20 mg three times a day, Metoprolol 25 mg every 12 hours, and Ticlid 250 mg twice a day.

**Test Done:** A specialized heart CT scan (called a coronary CTA) that checks for calcium buildup and heart function.

**Reason for Test:** Chest pain. 

**Medical History:** High cholesterol, overweight, chest pain, and a family history of heart disease.

**How the Test Was Done:** 
* The scan was done using a Siemens CT scanner and processed on a computer workstation.
* 150 mL of IV contrast dye (Ultravist 370) was used.
* The patient was given nitroglycerin under the tongue before getting the dye.

**Test Results:**
* **Calcium Score:** The patient's total Agatston calcium score is 10. This puts the patient just below the 75th percentile for their age.
* **Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery:** There is a moderate narrowing (stenosis) in the middle part of this artery caused by a hardened plaque. The beginning part of the artery is normal, but the far end could not be read.
* **Right Coronary Artery:** The middle and far sections of this artery could not be clearly seen due to image interference (beam-hardening artifact).
* **Circumflex Artery:** The beginning part of this artery is very small (diminutive). The far end could not be read.
* **Heart Movement:** The movement of the heart walls is normal.
* **Pulmonary Artery:** No obvious major problems were seen, though these arteries were not clearly detailed.

**Follow-up:** A full report was added to the patient's chart and saved in the computer system (PACS).

**Before Surgery Diagnosis:** Right inguinal hernia (a bulge in the right groin).
**After Surgery Diagnosis:** Direct right inguinal hernia.
**Surgery Performed:** Marlex mesh repair of the right inguinal hernia.
**Anesthesia:** Spinal block (medicine given in the back to numb the lower body).

**Details of the Surgery:**
The patient was brought to the operating room, laid flat on the table, and given a spinal anesthetic. The right groin area was shaved, cleaned, and covered with sterile drapes. The patient also received 1 gram of Ancef (an antibiotic) through an IV.

A cut was made in the groin crease, going through the skin and fat layer. The outer layer of tissue (external oblique fascia) was uncovered and cut down to the groin opening. The spermatic cord and the hernia sac were carefully separated from the tissue, revealing a weak spot in the floor of the groin canal. 

A rubber drain (Penrose drain) was placed around the cord, and the hernia sac was separated from the cord. The weak floor of the groin canal was folded over and stitched together using a continuous locking stitch. 

A 1-by-4-inch Marlex mesh patch was cut to the correct shape, with a hole made for the cord. The patch was wrapped around the cord, stitched to itself, and then sewn into place using Prolene stitches attached to the pubic bone, nearby ligaments, and a tendon. 

The area was washed with salt water (saline), and Marcaine with epinephrine (a numbing medicine) was injected to help control pain after surgery. The cord was put back in its normal place. 

The outer tissue layer was closed with stitches, the fat layer was closed with Vicryl stitches, and the skin was closed with a running hidden stitch and Steri-Strips (medical tape). The sponge and needle counts were checked and were correct. A sterile bandage was put on the wound.

**NEWBORN CIRCUMCISION PROCEDURE**

**Procedure Details:**
The procedure, risks, and benefits were explained to the baby's mother, and she signed a consent form. She understands the risks, which include bleeding, infection, narrowing of the urinary opening (meatal stenosis), removing too much or too little foreskin, and the possible need for a follow-up surgery in the future. 

The baby was placed on a support board (papoose board). His genital area was cleaned with Betadine. A pain-blocking shot (penile block) was given using a tiny needle (30-gauge) and 1.5 mL of Nesacaine (without epinephrine).

Next, the foreskin was clamped at the top (12 o'clock position) and cut. The skin stuck to the inside was gently separated. A special metal bell of the right size was placed over the head of the penis (glans). A Gomco clamp was attached, and the foreskin was pulled through it. The bell was put in place and tightened. Before doing this, the penis was checked all the way around to make sure no extra skin was bunched up, especially underneath. 

A surgical blade was used to cut the foreskin all the way around the bell. Then the bell was removed. There was no serious bleeding, and the result looked good with the correct amount of skin removed. 

Vaseline gauze was applied. The baby boy was then given back to his mother.

**Plan:**
The family has a newborn checkup coming soon with their regular doctor. I will see them again only if they have any problems with the circumcision.
